nodes.description: CNS xanthogranuloma produces no single syndrome. A dedicated series reports headache, seizure, ataxia, strabismus, hearing loss, facial paresis and diabetes insipidus.

evidence.reference_title: Neuroimaging in Pediatric Patients with Juvenile Xanthogranuloma of the CNS.
evidence.snippet: Patients presented with a wide variety of different symptoms, including headache, seizure, ataxia, strabismus, hearing loss, facial paresis, and diabetes insipidus.

nodes.description: A solitary yellow-orange papule or nodule, most often on the head and neck, appearing in infancy. It resolves without treatment in most patients.

evidence.reference_title: Genetic evaluation of juvenile xanthogranuloma: genomic abnormalities are uncommon in solitary lesions, advanced cases may show more complexity.
evidence.snippet: Juvenile xanthogranuloma is generally considered to be a benign disorder; most lesions are solitary cutaneous nodules that resolve spontaneously without treatment.

evidence.reference_title: Juvenile xanthogranulomas in Asian children.
evidence.snippet: Spontaneous resolution was documented in 57.7% of our patients with mean duration to resolution of 18.8 months.

nodes.description: Disease outside the skin, most often in the central nervous system, liver, lung or eye. A subset develops haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, with fever, rash, hepatosplenomegaly and cytopenia.

evidence.reference_title: Systemic juvenile xanthogranuloma: A systematic review.
evidence.snippet: The most commonly involved site was the central nervous system (CNS) (40.9%), followed by the liver (31.4%), the lung (18.9%), and the eye (18.2%).

evidence.reference_title: Clinical features and outcomes of 17 children with systemic juvenile xanthogranuloma (sJXG) including five complicated with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).
evidence.snippet: All sJXG-HLH patients had intermittent fever, rash, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenia and high levels of soluble CD25, but interferon-γ was almost normal.

nodes.description: Histiocyte-derived cells accumulate, usually in the skin and sometimes in soft tissue or viscera. This is the lesion itself.

evidence.reference_title: Genetic evaluation of juvenile xanthogranuloma: genomic abnormalities are uncommon in solitary lesions, advanced cases may show more complexity.
evidence.snippet: Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a rare histiocytic proliferation primarily affecting infants and young children, characterized by aberrant infiltration of histiocyte-derived cells in the skin, soft tissues and more rarely, visceral organs.

nodes.description: The driver alterations converge on three pathways - MAP kinase, PI3K and JAK/STAT - and the fusion-positive tumours additionally show mTOR activation and cyclin D1 expression.

evidence.reference_title: NTRK1 Gene Fusions Are Frequent in Juvenile Xanthogranuloma.
evidence.snippet: The most common known gene mutations affect the mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase, phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), and Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription ( JAK / STAT ) signaling pathways.

evidence.reference_title: Recurrent CLTC::SYK fusions and CSF1R mutations in juvenile xanthogranuloma of soft tissue.
evidence.snippet: Using multispectral immunofluorescence, phosphorylated-spleen tyrosine kinase expression was localized to CD163+ histiocytes; tumors with CLTC::SYK fusions also demonstrated mTOR activation, cyclin D1 expression, and variable phosphorylated-extracellular signal-regulated kinase expression.

nodes.description: The lesional histiocytes accumulate lipid and form the wreath-of-nuclei Touton giant cell that gives the lesion its name and its yellow colour. It is not obligate: tumours carrying a CLTC::SYK fusion generally lack Touton cells while otherwise looking like this disease.

evidence.reference_title: Juvenile xanthogranulomas in the first two decades of life: a clinicopathologic study of 174 cases with cutaneous and extracutaneous manifestations.
evidence.snippet: The characteristic Touton giant cell in variable numbers was a consistent feature of the cutaneous lesions; however, these cells were either absent or present in reduced numbers in the various extracutaneous lesions when compared with JXG in the skin.

evidence.reference_title: Recurrent CLTC::SYK fusions and CSF1R mutations in juvenile xanthogranuloma of soft tissue.
evidence.snippet: Tumors with CLTC::SYK fusions generally lacked Touton giant cells but exhibited many other histologic features of JXG and concordant methylation profiles.

evidence.reference_title: Recurrent CLTC::SYK fusions and CSF1R mutations in juvenile xanthogranuloma of soft tissue.
evidence.snippet: Finally, a TPM3::NTRK1 fusion or MAP2K1 deletion was detected in 2 children with systemic JXG who experienced spontaneous disease regression.

evidence.reference_title: NTRK1 Gene Fusions Are Frequent in Juvenile Xanthogranuloma.
evidence.snippet: In conclusion, NTRK1 gene fusions are moderately common in JXG (6/21; 28.6% in our series).

nodes.description: Ocular disease preferentially affects the iris and is often isolated, without any skin lesion. Redness and hyphema are the most common presenting signs, at 40 and 13 per cent of a 30-patient series.

evidence.reference_title: Juvenile Xanthogranuloma Involving the Eye and Ocular Adnexa: Tumor Control, Visual Outcomes, and Globe Salvage in 30 Patients.
evidence.snippet: Eye redness (12/30, 40%) and hyphema (4/30, 13%) were the most common presenting symptoms.

evidence.reference_title: Juvenile Xanthogranuloma Involving the Eye and Ocular Adnexa: Tumor Control, Visual Outcomes, and Globe Salvage in 30 Patients.
evidence.snippet: Ocular JXG preferentially affects the iris and is often isolated without cutaneous involvement.

nodes.description: The initiating lesion is a somatic, activating alteration in a kinase gene, in a cell of the macrophage/dendritic lineage. The series that establishes this is scoped to the rare extracutaneous form: it found a targetable kinase alteration in 16 of 16 children with extracutaneous disease, CLTC::SYK fusion and CSF1R mutation commonest, with NTRK1 fusion, BRAF V600E and MAP2K1 deletion also represented. The lesion's clonality has been shown; which cell it arises in has not been settled, and the entry records that as the open question it is.

evidence.reference_title: BRAF V600E mutation in pediatric intracranial and cranial juvenile xanthogranuloma.
evidence.snippet: The lesion is presumed to originate from either macrophages or dermal dendritic cells.

evidence.reference_title: Juvenile xanthogranulomas in the first two decades of life: a clinicopathologic study of 174 cases with cutaneous and extracutaneous manifestations.
evidence.snippet: It is widely held that JXG is a proliferative disorder of dendrocytes, possibly dermal dendrocytes; thus, its clinical and pathologic similarities to Langerhans cell histiocytosis are not entirely unexpected in light of the most recently proposed international classification of histiocytic disorders, which includes JXG and Langerhans cell histiocytosis together as "dendritic cell-related" histiocytoses.

evidence.snippet: The presence of non-recurrent copy number alterations in a subset of samples implies that copy number changes are unlikely driving pathogenesis in juvenile xanthogranuloma, but may be acquired during disease progression.
